utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the microphone of the registrar is not functioning. Could you please, just for calling the case, use another microphone? Or are they all -- mine is working. Mr. Registrar, you are invited to use mine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I do understand that most of the microphones are not working. This should be fixed, because I take it that the Prosecution has problems in continuing with its opening statement if the microphones are not working.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they are working, so then let's proceed. The Chamber has been informed by the Registry that Mr. Seselj did not wish to come to court, or was unable to come to court, but at least that he did not -- that he expressed that he would not appear. We have a few procedural matters, but I'd rather leave them until after the Prosecution has finished its opening statement. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, 50 minutes, I said yesterday, 50.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That takes you until 10.00. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will now move on to another group of victims and another group of crimes, and there is -- I don't have a map. You see here the map again, this map number 2 in the binder. I would like to direct your attention to Mostar and Nevesinje in southern Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those municipalities were relevant for the goal in relation to the Neretva River and the access to the sea. In addition, Mostar was important because it had two large military barracks, an airport and other military facilities. A young Muslim boy, who happily lived with his family in a small Muslim village in the Nevesinje municipality, saw his calm rural world fall apart in June 1992. The family had not done anything wrong, were not involved in politics or military matters, and felt safe in Nevesinje, a municipality with a Serb majority population, firmly under control of the Serb forces. The family felt safe even when other Muslims started hiding in the woods and leaving. In June 1992, the boy's family was the last to flee the village, realising that Muslims were not safe in Nevesinje, and innocent civilians were killed, houses destroyed, and villages shelled. The boy, with his parents, grandparents, little brothers, and other relatives, tried to flee in the direction of Mostar but they were captured by Serb soldiers. They were taken to a detention facility in the village of Zijemlje and there, the terrified children had to see and hear their relatives being beaten and tortured. The three children then were separated from their parents and grandparents. This is the last time the children saw their parents and relatives because they were taken away and murdered. Their bodies were later discovered in a pit. The children continued to be detained, first in Zijemlje and then in the basement of SUP building in Nevesinje, under unbearable conditions. They were joined by four more very small children and two old women. After about 15 days of detention, this group of terrified children and these old women were taken in the direction of Stolac and dropped off by Serb soldiers in the middle of nowhere. They were eventually saved by Croat soldiers. Having lost their parents and grandparents, the children, after the war, grew up in a children's home. One of them will be a witness here. Their fate is only one of the many examples of human suffering in Nevesinje and Mostar. The Prosecution will provide evidence from victims, soldiers and experts about several mass murders committed in June 1992 in Mostar and Nevesinje by the Serb forces; namely, the murder of 88 Muslim civilians on the 13th of June at the Ubarak city dump in Mostar; the murder of 18 non-Serb civilians at the city mortuary in Sutina, in Mostar, on that same day; the murder of more than 70 civilians that were captured on the flight from Nevesinje on the 22nd of June, 1992, among them many children, many women and old people; the murder of two women that were detained and assaulted at Boracko Jezero. The Prosecution will also provide evidence on other crimes committed by Serb forces, including sexual assault, in particular at that same lake. Why does the Prosecution hold the accused responsible? Prior to the war, neither the SRS party, nor the SCP movement had a noticeable presence in Mostar. However, in the neighbouring Nevesinje, Arsen Grahovac promoted the SCP ideology. From 1991 onwards, his pub, Ravna Gora, became a gathering point for SCP and SRS members and sympathisers. Grahovac established a unit called Karadjordje. This unit was comprised of between 80 and 100 members and sympathisers of the SCP and the SRS, and operated both in Mostar and Nevesinje. The group commanded by Grahovac was not the only group of volunteers associated with the accused Seselj. From autumn 1991, in particular in 1992, SRS and SCP volunteers from Serbia and Montenegro and from the battlefields in Croatia arrived. These volunteers were commanded by Branislav Vakic, the man I mentioned already in relation to Vukovar, and Radovan Radovic. In mid-May 1992, Mostar was taken over by Serb forces comprised of JNA, Serb TO, SRS/SCP volunteers, Red Berets from the Serbian DB, in an offensive commanded by General Momcilo Perisic. We will hear from the participants in the attack that Oliver Baret, one of the leading SRS/SCP commanders who had close connections to the SRS leadership, arrived from Belgrade and was present in the military headquarters of the JNA headquarters in Mostar, communicating constantly with the SRS volunteer units. SRS/SCP volunteers were among the troops that, in June 1992, attacked the Muslim villages and settlements in the Nevesinje municipality, too. In the persecution that took place in Mostar and Nevesinje, SRS and SCP volunteers figured prominently among those abusing the non-Serb population. These volunteers were involved in every murder and every abuse that I just mentioned to you in both locations. And again, we have the accused visiting the conflict area during the events. And again, we have the promotion of those commanders involved in the crimes. To save time, I'm not showing you the promotion order, Exhibit 2015, the order 124, any longer, but we find again the promotion Vakic. But I will show you now another promotion order, and it is from the 20th of March, 1994. It is very similar. If you look at -- if you look at the top of it, you can actually see again that the Vojvoda Seselj is actually promoting the others mentioned below. And below, as number 2, is mentioned Radovic; he is mentioned for his participation in Dubrovnik and in the Neretva valley, which includes Nevesinje. And as number 5, we have Oliver Baret; he is mentioned as a Chetnik Major, one of the founders of the SCP being involved throughout Croatia, beginning in Borovo Selo, going to Okucani in Western Slavonia, and finally in Herzegovina; namely, in Mostar. This indictment also deals with events in Sarajevo; however, we are not concerned in this trial with the shelling and sniping of Sarajevo. Instead, the indictment depicts crimes committed by some of the closest associates of the accused; namely, Vasilije Vidovic, Slavko Aleksic, and Branislav Gavrilovic, who later were praised by the accused and promoted for their conduct in Sarajevo. At the outset, let me just show you a map. That is Sarajevo, and those red parts in there, these are the municipalities we are concerned with in this trial - Ilijas, Vogosca, Ilidza and Novo Sarajevo. The accused promoted, on the 20th of March, 1994, and that's the order you just saw, the order number -- Exhibit 2288, he promoted Vasilije Vidovic for his achievements in this greater Sarajevo area. The accused promoted a man who, on the 5th of June, 1992, together with his men, murdered 22 Muslims civilians of Ljecevvo, both men and women. The accused promoted a man whose subordinates murdered prisoners of war in the summer of 1993 in Crna Rijeka, and who cut off the head of a civilian there; and also, in the summer of 1993, murdered 27 Muslim detainees as a revenge for Serb losses at the front line. Seselj promoted a man who detained many non-Serb civilians in various detention facilities in Ilijas and Vogosca municipalities over extended periods of times, and subjected them to the abuse, including beatings, torture, rape, forced labour under dangerous conditions on the front lines, and killings. Vasilije Vidovic originated from Ilijas. In 1991, he organised a group of SRS/SCP volunteers and spent time with them at the front lines in Croatia where he already was involved in murders in the SAO Krajina. When the conflict started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Vidovic returned with his men to Sarajevo. He was in close contact and cooperated with the local SDS Crisis Staff. He and his men could do whatever they wanted with impunity. We will hear from witnesses that Vasilije Vidovic was a particularly brutal and ruthless man, who drove around in a jeep with a human skull on the hood. He and his men were rightly known for their brutality and the murder of the civilians and prisoners of war. Despite all this, Vidovic remained a close associate of the accused. The accused would come to Ilijas and meet him and his men, and as well, Vidovic went to Belgrade and met the accused. Vidovic remained close to the accused even after the war and acted as his bodyguard. Let me now turn to another of these close associates. You see here a photo of Slavko Aleksic, in the middle of this photograph. He and his SRS/SCP volunteers controlled the area of the Jewish cemetery in Grbavica. He was also promoted, again, in that order of the -- order number 124, and he was referred in this order as the Commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik detachment. After the war, the accused praised Aleksic and the SRS volunteers in Grbavica, saying they had performed a great service to the SRS and the Serb nationalism. What did Slavko Aleksic do for the Serb cause? He and his men subjected the non-Serbs in Grbavica to a persecution campaign which included arbitrary searches of homes, looting, rapes, beatings and killings. Both men and women were subjected to forced labour under dangerous reasons, and more than 80 civilians were killed while performing forced labour. Finally, Branislav Gavrilovic, also known as Brne, he was also active in the greater Sarajevo area. Gavrilovic became the leader of the Serbian youth movement of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an organisation that joined the accused's SRS/SCP movement after Gavrilovic had met the accused in Bijeljina in 1991. The accused appointed him later to be the commander of the volunteers in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. And you actually see here Exhibit 1258, a certificate signed by the accused and Ljubisa Petkovic, confirming that Gavrilovic just had this position in the time period from June to December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, when I follow the French translation, I see that they are quite a few lines behind. Could you please slow down. I do not know whether, for the B/C/S translation, we have a similar problem. But if you slow down a bit, then the interpreters will be better able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will just first check with the French translation where we are. I am still waiting in French for the translation of my own words where I asked Madam Uertz-Retzlaff to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's been done. It's already been translated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Gavrilovic was also one of the leaders of the SRS party in Ilidza. During the war, he was in charge of a huge unit of volunteers. The Prosecution will provide evidence that Gavrilovic, while in Croatia and also later in Bosnia and Herzegovina, would receive orders from the SRS office in Belgrade, and he would meet the accused frequently, both in Belgrade and in Sarajevo. He was also appointed Vojvoda in May 1993, in that order number 124. I'll show you just a photo now. Branislav Gavrilovic is the second man from the left. Let me give you one example of what Gavrilovic -- by the way, yes, it's the second from the left counting all the men, where there is no name given. Let me give you an example of what Gavrilovic did in Sarajevo. On the 17th of July, 1993, Branislav Gavrilovic and his SRS/SCP volunteers captured four members of the Sarajevo TO on their position in Golo Brdo at Mount Igman, facing Ilidza. They shot one of them, a 17-year-old boy, on the spot. The other prisoners of war were interrogated by Gavrilovic and one of his subordinates. During the interrogation, they were hit, beaten and kicked. Two of the prisoners of war were, afterwards, murdered. The crimes that I just described were committed because the accused and the other members of the JCE wanted to achieve Serb domination in particular territories in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and a lot of innocent people had to pay a heavy price for that. But, Your Honours, let me now turn to my colleague, Mr. Saxon, who will address some particular aspects of the role of the accused and the crimes committed in Serbia itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you tell me precisely how many minutes the Prosecution has remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thirty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thirty-two minutes. I will endeavour to finish my remarks in 32 minutes. I may ask you for, perhaps, a couple of minutes more but I will try not to do that. Your Honours, this trial, perhaps more than any other case before this Tribunal, is about the use of words, language and expression. This trial is about the use of political speech to poison the minds of men and women in order to further criminal goals. This case is about the ability of the accused, Vojislav Seselj, to use propaganda to condition Serbs to fear, hate, and commit violence against members of the non-Serb communities in the former Yugoslavia, in particular, Croats and Muslims. One simple definition of "propaganda" is "an endeavour to spread ideas without regard to truth or to accuracy." Massive crimes, such as the mass murders and the expulsions of entire communities from their homes lying at the heart of this case, require the assistance of persons who believe that the atrocities they commit are justified, necessary, and immune to any sanction. Prior to the 1990s, ethnic relations between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims in the former Yugoslavia were relatively good. To change that situation, to convince Serbs to accept or to carry out acts of violence and destruction necessary to achieve the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise described by my colleague, to forcibly expel thousands of non-Serbs from their homes, the propaganda used by political elites had to be extreme. And so it was. This war, Your Honours, was fought with words in addition to arms. I'd like to briefly show you an excerpt from some video footage taken on the 17th of April, 1991, at a place called Plitvice, in Croatia. This is Prosecution Exhibit 3155.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "JOURNALIST: In such an atmosphere, vojvoda Seselj announced already at the beginning of the meeting, started his speech. AUDIENCE: Voja! Voja! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! Serbia! VOJISLAV SESELJ: Here Serbian people live, this is Serbian land and it will remain Serbian forever. AUDIENCE: That's right! That's right! JOURNALIST: Instead of calming then down, Seselj sent a message to the gathered people at the end. VOJISLAV SESELJ: We are sending a message to the new Ustasha head of state and Ustasha regime in Croatia: Serbian heads have rolled, struck down by the Ustasha hand in the Serbian Krajina. A Serbian head has rolled down in Serbian Western Srem and Slavonia, as well - we will avenge Serbian blood. AUDIENCE: We will."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That last sentence by the accused would be prophetic. Without the extraordinary communication skills of this accused and other politicians like him, without Seselj's ability and determination to inculcate his version of reality into the minds of many Serbs, there would have been very few so-called foot soldiers to carry out the violent goals of the joint criminal enterprise. There would have been very few foot soldiers to accomplish the accused's personal goal of the creation of the Greater Serbia. This next video clip was made on the 21st of April, 1991, and it shows the accused speaking in the town of Jagodnjak, in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "As far as we are concerned, the Croats can leave Yugoslavia any time they want, but we are letting them know openly that they will not take an inch of Serbian territory, not a piece of land on which there are Serbian villages, demolished churches, caves in which Serbs were butchered, Serbian camps, Serbian killing fields, such as Jasenovac. Should we permit that, we would be unworthy of our glorious ancestors and shamed before our descendants. The Croats may create their new state, but only to the west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Everything to the east of that line ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is well aware of the tension that exists --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Could we have an exhibit number for that, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 724, clip B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hooper, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I just asked the exhibit number; 724, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution is well aware of the tension that exists between the internationally recognised right of freedom of expression, in particular, the right to express political ideas, and the use of hate speech which forms one of the basis for holding the accused criminally responsible for the charges alleged in the indictment. This is not the first international prosecution of an accused for the criminal use of propaganda. Following the Second World War, the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg convicted Julius Streicher of the crime against humanity of persecution for his incitement of the German people to murder and exterminate the Jews. Just as Julius Streicher continued to publish his so-called propaganda of death, with full knowledge of the extermination of the Jews in the occupied eastern territory, Seselj used demonising and dehumanising rhetoric about non-Serbs during the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia, with knowledge of the crimes being committed by Serb forces that were a direct result of his propaganda and speeches. Julius Streicher's advocacy of "the final solution" during the Second World War was considered a general campaign of persecution not linked to specific acts and conduct. In this case, Seselj's participation in the joint criminal enterprise, through his propaganda of fear and hatred directed against non-Serbs, also amounted to a similar general persecution campaign. But in addition, Seselj, through his use of propaganda, directly instigated specific crimes at specific sites and personally committed specific crimes at specific sites. Given his position in Serbian society, Seselj possessed the dangerous ability to broadcast his propaganda and exert his influence in both the political and military arenas simultaneously. This enabled him to recruit and indoctrinate persons willing to wage war and commit the crimes necessary to further his goal of the establishment of Greater Serbia. I'd like to show you another short video clip. It's from Prosecution Exhibit 747. It shows the accused speaking before the Serbian parliament in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica has to be our goal, and that is the border where the army has to withdraw its troops. If the army is unable to move its troops from Zagreb to this line without a fight, then they should do this with force and with the bombing of Zagreb. The army still has capacities which it has not yet used. If its troops are endangered, it has the right to use napalm bombs and anything else they have available in their warehouses. We cannot play games here. It is more important to save one army unit than to worry if there will be some accidental victims. Who is to blame here? They wanted war. Now they have it."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the judgement of the so-called "Media Trial," the ICTR convicted Ferdinand Nahimana, Jean-Bosco Barayagwiza, and Hassan Ngeze for the crimes of direct and public incitement to commit genocide and the crime against humanity of persecution. The ICTR Trial Chamber focused on the cumulative impact of the hate speech and incitement to violence emanating from the newspaper articles in "Kangura" and the RTLM radio programmes broadcast throughout Rwanda. In this case, using examples and the expert evidence of Dr. Anthony Oberschall, the Prosecution will likewise demonstrate the cumulative effect of Seselj's propaganda. What makes this case distinct and separate from the "Media Case," however, is the fact that Seselj personally committed the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer with his public speeches. Please bear in mind an important point developed by the "Media" judgement. In paragraphs 1008 and 1009, the Trial Chamber observed that the dangers of censorship are often associated with the suppression of minorities or groups who are in opposition to the government. These circumstances do not arise in the case of Mr. Seselj's use of political expression between August 1991 and September 1993 because Mr. Seselj was advocating on behalf of the majority population of Serbia and in support of the ruling Milosevic regime and its police and military forces. No issue exists in these proceedings of an infringement of a minority's right to express itself. International human rights treaties recognise the tensions that may exist between the right to freedom of expression and other fundamental human rights. The judgements from the European Court of Human Rights provide some guidance as to when so-called "fighting words," the expression of tough, even violent communications in a democratic marketplace of ideas, cross the frontier between lawful and illegal speech. The determining factor in this jurisprudence, discussing whether political speech can be legitimately restricted, is: Does the speech or communication constitute incitement to violence or is it capable of inciting violence? I might respectfully direct Your Honours' attention to the judgement in the case of Surek vs. Turkey, issued on the 8th of July, 1992, pages 27 to 28. In a concurring opinion to a different judgement issued on the same day, Surek and Ozdemir vs. Turkey, at page 40 of the English version, five judges of the European Court of Human Rights suggested that less attention should be given to the form of words used and more attention directed to the general context in which the words were used and their likely impact. Was the language intended to inflame or incite to violence? Was there a real and genuine risk that it might actually do so? Did the author of the offending text occupy a position of influence in society of a sort likely to amplify the impact of his words? Was the publication given a degree of prominence either in an important newspaper or through another medium which was likely to enhance the influence of the impugned speech? Were the words far away from the centre of violence or on its doorstep? Your Honours, this concurring opinion represents a more nuanced and rigorous test for legitimate restrictions on speech than the more general criteria applied by a majority of the judges of the ECHR. But should the Trial Chamber decide to apply this more rigorous test to the evidence of Seselj's propaganda presented in this case, it will see that even under this higher level of scrutiny, this accused's speech was criminal. The Prosecution's expert witness, Dr. Anthony Oberschall, will identify a number of topics and methods of persuasion which served to make the accused's propaganda particularly effective; for example, the idea that the Serbian population is threatened and in danger. By the spring and summer of 1991, Vojislav Seselj increasingly used his exceptional rhetorical skills to convince Serbs that members of other nationalities, particularly Croats, posed a grave danger to the survival of Serbs as a group. Seselj referred to Croats as Ustasha, to link all Croats to the fascist regime that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II. I'd like to briefly show you a clip. This is Prosecution Exhibit 755. This was originally part of the BBC documentary "The Death of Yugoslavia," and it shows the accused speaking in front of the Federal Assembly in Belgrade during the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The very roots of the Serbian cause are under threat. Hoards of Ustashas are attacking Serbian villages, Serbian women and children. The Ustasha hordes are trying to finalise the genocide of the Serbian nation."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Another rhetorical tool used by Seselj was the constant depiction of the Serb population as victims of past and present crimes committed by Croats and other nationalities. Seselj skillfully used that sense of victimhood as justification for acts of collective violence and revenge, including the loss of territories. This next video comes, again, from Exhibit 724, part of the speech on the 21st of April, 1991, at Jagodnjak, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we play that, Mr. Saxon, I get the impression that the portions of the video you're drawing our attention to are translated. They may be on paper, as part of your opening statement, which may have been provided to the translators, but I also heard there's an English introduction before Mr. Seselj speaks. I don't know whether that's on paper. I don't know whether this English introduction is also translated in B/C/S; I didn't check that. If it has not been translated, then it -- this should be corrected, because that's part of what we hear in English. That should be translated in B/C/S as well. May I ask the B/C/S booth, and I'll change it to, whether you have translated the English introduction. Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, we haven't translated that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the way it should be done, Mr. Saxon. If anything is played in English here, as an introduction, even if you did not write that down, perhaps, as part of your opening statement, it came to our ears, it therefore -- I invite you to play that last video portion again and I'd like to invite the B/C/S booth, and, of course, the same is true for the French booth, to translate also the introduction given by the reporter and not only that portion you consider to be relevant for your opening statement, because it came to our ears in English; it has to come to everyone's ears listening to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will do that now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We will do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "JOURNALIST: To this end, extremist allies of President Milosevic set about provoking a conflict between Serbs and Croats."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The very roots of Serbdom are under threat. Hordes of Ustashas are attacking Serb villages, Serb women and children. The Ustasha hordes are trying to finalise the genocide of the Serbian nation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Another rhetorical tool used by Vojislav Seselj was the constant depiction of the Serb population as victims of past and present crimes committed by Croats and other nationalities. He skillfully used that sense of victimhood as justification for acts of collective violence and revenge, including the loss of territories. This next video clip comes, again, from Exhibit 724. It's from the accused's speech in Jagodnjak, Croatia, in April 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The new Ustasha chief and Josip Broz's general Franjo Tudjman, and the new Ustasha government in Croatia have again put the kama under its throat. Should they attempt a new genocide against the Serb people, we say to them we shall take revenge for each Serb life and we shall also ask to pay up for past crimes ... also for crimes in recent history. No deed will be unpunished. And we will not allow ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Seselj's speeches demonised and dehumanised Croats, Muslims and other non-Serbs by portraying them using negative stereotypes, by linking all Croats to the fascist Ustasha regime, by labelling Bosniaks as supporters of the fundamentalist pan-Islamist movements that allegedly intended to take control of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The next exhibit is from 569 and it's part of the interview that the accused gave to a magazine called "On" on the 24th of May, 1991. The accused said on that day, among other things, "How is one supposed to negotiate with the Ustashas? Did you see today that the Croatian people are entirely Ustasha? There are very few exceptions." By demonising and dehumanising Croats and Muslims, Seselj's speeches removed any need to question the morality or legality of crimes committed against non-Serbs. At the same time, Seselj's speeches glorified the Serb people and their behaviour in wartime, further encouraging aggression and violence against other national groups. This next exhibit that you will see in front of you is from Prosecution Exhibit 1836. It's an excerpt from an article that was published in the newspaper of the Serbian Radical Party, Velika Serbia, No. 10, from 1991, and it records the accused saying, with respect to the Croatian Serbs: "We greet their heroic leader, Milan Babic, who is in the front lines of the defence of Serbdom, whose intelligence and courage have placed him amongst the greatest sons of the Serbian people. And we would tell him that thousands of Chetniks will jump to his aid every time he seeks help. We also greet the SDS of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its clever leader, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, who stood in the front lines in the defence of national interests through the will of the Serbian people. We would tell them all that they will not stand alone as long as Serbian Chetniks are ready to follow the glorious example of their forebears." And so continued the process of conditioning large segments of the Serb population that they were endangered, that Croats and other non-Serbs were persons to be feared and hated, and that action, including extreme action, had to be taken quickly to destroy this grave threat to Serbs. Several aspects of the accused's use of language from 1991 to 1993 made his form of political speech criminal. First, Vojislav Seselj used his particular forms of expression within a volatile context of war and political turmoil, when members of all national and ethnic communities would be highly susceptible to his messages of fear and hate. Second, Seselj was fully aware of his own political power and his extraordinary ability to influence people through his speeches. Statements made by the accused for the BBC's film "The Death of Yugoslavia," as well as statements made by Seselj during his testimony in the Milosevic trial, are illustrative. The next two video clips come from "The Death of Yugoslavia," Your Honour, which is Prosecution Exhibit 756.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Milan Babic came with me and the people booed him, but then I gave a fiery speech and then people started applauding. Milan Babic wanted to reconcile with Raskovic, but Raskovic refused on the spot, and that's why he failed politically." "I first went there on the 9th of March, while Vuk Draskovic was destroying Belgrade here in the protests against the Serb -- the regime. I went to Slavonia to raise an uprising of the Serbian people. I am honoured by the role I had in 1991. The Serbs there asked for me, they called me. First of all, they did not trust Milosevic much. He was giving them promises which he did not always fulfill. They felt threatened, and because we at the Serb Chetnik movement gathered a large number of decisive, capable and courageous people, they asked for our help."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next exhibit comes from Prosecution Exhibit, I believe it's, 2828, the testimony of Mr. Seselj during the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. This is from the accused's testimony on the 24th of August, 2005, page 43125, where His Honour Judge Bonomy asked Mr. Seselj, then a witness: "JUDGE BONOMY: Mr. Seselj, how many volunteers were there from the Serb Radical Party?" And Seselj responded: "THE WITNESS: Well, sort of for propaganda reasons, we said that there were about 30.000 of them, but the real figure would have been about 10.000." Thus, the Prosecution's evidence will prove that when Seselj used political speech to generate fear and hatred amongst different nationalities, his actions were calculated and deliberate. Third, by demonising and denigrating the non-Serb population, Seselj's speeches, in the minds of his listeners, justified their acts of violence committed against non-Serbs and helped to make such acts permissible. Fourth, such hate speech by Seselj, per se, harmed the human dignity of non-Serbs in the former Yugoslavia and thereby constituted a form of persecution. Fifth, as my colleague told you, Seselj's speeches directly instigated and incited Serb men and women to commit acts of violence against non-Serbs. Sixth, Seselj, through his speeches promoting fear and hatred of non-Serbs, personally committed the crimes against humanity of deportation and forcible transfer. Seselj's criminal forms of public expression were highly effective in the province of Vojvodina, Serbia, home to more than 72.000 ethnic Serb-Croats prior to the start of the war. Your Honours, I must interrupt my speech now. I see that I will shortly be arriving, formally at least, at the 32-minute mark. If I were to read the rest of my speech and present the selected exhibits, I believe it would take approximately ten more minutes, perhaps a bit longer. I need some guidance from the Trial Chamber as to how much time you will indulge me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, the Chamber decides that you get another ten minutes; that means until 12 minutes past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This map in front of you is map number 20 in the binder of maps that you received yesterday, and it shows in the middle, it shows the province known as Vojvodina, the province of Serbia known as Vojvodina. You see Belgrade at the south and you see the town of Hrtkovci, a red dot just to the north-west of Belgrade. Vojvodina is the province of Serbia which borders Croatia; namely, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. Eventually, Vojvodina would become the Serbian Radical Party stronghold, and the accused visited different locations in Vojvodina on numerous occasions. As you will hear from Prosecution expert witness Ewa Tabeau, during 1991 and 1992, close to 250.000 ethnic Serb refugees came to Serbia from Croatia and parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. More than 95.000 of these ethnic Serb refugees arrived in Vojvodina, some of them in buses arranged by the Serbian Radical Party. To make room for these refugees and to further his own political agenda, the accused spoke at rallies, at private meetings, and in the Serbian parliament, calling for the expulsion of Croats from Vojvodina. He declared Croats to be disloyal citizens who had to be expelled. For the assistance of my case manager and those following -- the interpreters following along in the booth, I'm going to jump forward in my speech. I'm going to ignore Exhibit 745 and 612. The ethnic Croats then living in the farming village of Hrtkovci, about an hour's drive north-west of Belgrade, were some of the victims of Vojislav Seselj's campaign to drive Croats out of Serbia. Tensions began to rise in Hrtkovci during the second half of 1991 with the arrival of Serb refugees in that community. Serbs from outside Hrtkovci, as well as Serb residents of that village associated with the Serbian Radical Party, harassed and threatened some prominent Croat residents and told them to leave the village. On the 6th of May, 1992, Seselj spoke at a public rally in Hrtkovci organized by the Serbian Radical Party. Prosecution witnesses will describe how Seselj called for the expulsion of Croats from that community. What you're seeing now on your screen is an excerpt from Prosecution Exhibit 556. This is from the speech that Seselj gave in Hrtkovci on that day. It was reprinted in one of his books, "The Devil's Apprentice, Criminal Roman Pope John Paul II." And we see that Seselj said the following in the first paragraph: "In this village, too, in Hrtkovci, in this place in Serbian Srem, there is no room for Croats. Who are those Croats for whom there is room among us? Only those Croats and their families who have shed blood together with us on the front lines. They were called Croats in name only, anyway. Some of them served with our volunteers. They have already awakened to the fact that they are, in fact, Catholic Serbs. They will stay here with us while all the rest must clear out of Serbia." And then in the next paragraph, lower down, it says in the middle of the next paragraph: "Very well, then, if we cannot do that, then we should give every Serbian family of refugees the address of one Croatian family. The police will give it to them, the police will do as the government decides, and we will be the government soon. Fine, then. Every Serbian family of refugees will knock on one Croatian door and give whatever Croats they find their address in Zagreb or another Croatian place. Oh, they will, they will. There will be enough buses, we will drive them to the border of Serbian territory, and they can walk on from there, if they do not leave before of their own accord." And later on, another paragraph, the accused told the assembled crowd: "I firmly believe that you, Serbs from Hrtkovci and other villages and here, will also know how to preserve your harmony and unity, that you will promptly get rid of the remaining Croats in your village and the surrounding villages." The Prosecution witnesses will then describe the fear caused by Seselj's speech and the subsequent expulsion campaign of ethnic Croats in the village of Hrtkovci, which, to a large degree, mirrored the instructions given in Seselj's speech. I'm now going to skip forward some more to page 18, paragraph 27. The evidence will demonstrate that Seselj used all available media resources: television, radio, daily newspapers, including two Serbian Radical Party newspapers, one printed in Belgrade and the other in Banja Luka, weekly periodicals and personal appearances to disseminate his hate speech. The cartoon you see on your screen is Prosecution Exhibit 0666. Even cartoons were used to spread messages attacking non-Serbs and glorifying violence against Croats and Muslims. This cartoon was published in the July 1993 issue of "Western Serbia", one of the Radical Party's newspapers. This cartoon was published next to an article entitled "There is No Co-Existence with Islam." The cartoon depicts a large Serb Orthodox church and a man with a broom who is sweeping small mosques away from the area around the church. The Prosecution's evidence will demonstrate that by the time this disgusting cartoon was published, the message it promoted, the destruction of Muslim cultural property as a means of destroying Muslim identity and presence, had already been fulfilled in many communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm now at paragraph 29. It is reasonable to ask how mere words spoken and written by Vojislav Seselj, broadcast on radio and television and published in newspapers and in the accused's numerous books, could incite so many people to commit so many horrible crimes. Your Honours, the answer lies in the very ordinariness of human nature. Professor Anthony Oberschall will explain to the Chamber how every human being is susceptible to the conditioning rhetoric of fear and how it is but a very small emotional step from the common human condition of fear to the poisonous mentality of hate. Recent history contains many tragic examples of how ordinary people, people like you and I, under certain circumstances, can be persuaded to commit the most terrible acts. That's why some of the Prosecution evidence will also focus on the ordinary Serb men and women, many of them young and just starting their lives, who believed in Vojislav Seselj's message and followed his leadership by taking up arms, going off to war, and who committed acts of brutality. In the time I have left, Your Honours, first, I would like to show you some video footage of those young volunteers, men and women. The first footage comes from Prosecution Exhibit 2875. It's from a documentary called "The City of Lost Souls."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: Miso. "UNIDENTIFIED CHETNIK: A Chetnik, a Chetnik, remember. UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: Hey, Miso ... Miso ... Miso ... We'll be Serb. It will be ours. There will be no more fascism. We will no longer allow it. And they hated us. It is enough now, the end." UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: [In English] We can only fight with them. JOURNALIST: Why? UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: [In English] Why? Because they kill our people, they kill our children. You have never seen the kid of 2 years old with head -- with the head of the kid is on the pig, you know, and the head of the pig is on the kid's body. You know what that means? Have you ever seen that? No? With that people you discuss? Never. Only fight, to the end, the last -- the last bullet, the last Ustasha, you know." "[Interpretation] Let's go back to the company. Let's go."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, not all wars or acts of combat are illegal, but Seselj's war of words was criminal for one fundamental reason. This accused exercised his right to expression for a criminal purpose: to spread fear, hate, violence and suffering in the former Yugoslavia, in an attempt to establish a single Serbian state, his Greater Serbia. For this reason, and for all of the reasons that I have mentioned, Seselj deserves to be held accountable for crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. This concludes the opening statement of the Prosecution, I take it, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Mr. Hooper, yesterday, when I asked you whether there would be any opening statement, you said you could not at that moment make an opening statement, and we are aware that Mr. Seselj preferred to delay the opening statement; that's what he told us before. Is there any new development in this respect that you'd like to report to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Well, since yesterday, we've had no contact with Dr. Seselj, so I'm not able, in fact, to add anything in respect of that. There's certainly no intent on my part, as I indicated yesterday, to address you this morning by way of an opening statement. Rather, I seek to preserve Dr. Seselj's opportunity to do so at a later time, and I sincerely hope, as I indicated yesterday, that that time will arrive. So I'm not going to make any opening submissions for the Defence. But for all that, it may be appropriate for me to say just a few general words because of the particular and perhaps unusual position that I, as assigned counsel, find myself in, and as we, as now his assigned Defence team find ourselves in, and I won't take up very many minutes, if you'd give me that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that opportunity is given to you, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Seselj, of course, is not here, and the reason that I am here, as I think we all know, is because, of course, you, the Judges, supported by the view of the Judges of the Appeal Chamber, took the view that Dr. Seselj was being needlessly obstructive, and that in behaving in that way - and I don't go into it any further than that - he was deemed not to be acting in either his own interests nor that of the interests of justice. And the view was taken by the Chamber, as I say, supported by the Appeal Chamber, that in those circumstances, his right to self-represent would be withdrawn from him, and I, together with Dr. O'Shea and the others who are now assigned, would form his Defence team. It was felt, in short, that in the absence of his representation of himself, some counsel was felt to be better than no counsel, but it's not - and we all recognise this - an ideal situation; it's far from ideal. And I know that both I and the other members of the assigned team, together with you, the Judges, would much prefer that Dr. Seselj play as full a part as possible in this, his trial, and for very good reason. Dr. Seselj is, after all, charged with the most serious offences and the most serious charges, as we've heard, that have just been outlined by the Prosecution yesterday and this morning. He's pleaded not guilty to those offences. Indeed, it's right to say that he brought himself here to The Hague and surrendered himself here to The Hague in order to meet those allegations and charges. For all that's been said this morning, and for all that's been said from time to time in the media over the last several years, it's not for him, we remind ourselves, to prove his innocence. He has not to prove that he did not do what is alleged. The Prosecution have charged him and brought the indictment against him, and it's for them, obviously, to prove, and to a high standard, that he's committed those offences, and to prove them, in short, up to the hilt. And this man we know, we all know, because it is our jurisprudence, is at this stage presumed innocent of these charges. So as we start this trial, it's very important that you, the Judges, remind yourselves that this man is at this stage to be presumed innocent of these charges and that your prejudices at this stage should be for him and not against him. Now, he's not here. He should be here. It's essential that he play as full a role in this, his trial, as he possibly can. It is, after all, the only trial he is probably going to get, and he knows that, I should think. He's an intelligent and perceptive man. He is a brave man, too, from acts that we've seen recorded that he's done over the years. And I hope that he can find the courage to lay aside his exasperations, many of which may, perhaps, be justified, to lay those aside and to come and confront his accusers, because I cannot do that alone. But I stress that it lies in his hands and in nobody else's hands whether this trial is to have the allegations met fully with his participation and whether this trial is going to reach the successful conclusion that he wishes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hooper. You told us that the present situation is far from ideal, and in two different lines, you said once that you'd like Mr. Seselj to play a role, as full a role as possible, or at another moment you said to play a part, as full as possible. The Chamber agrees with that and the Chamber thanks you at this moment for the observations you just made. Then a few procedural matters before we will adjourn. First of all, the Chamber received from the representative of the Registry the message that Mr. Van der Spoel has been approached and that talks are held to see whether he could take the role the Chamber had in mind when giving its decision yesterday. The second issue: The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution might not pursue its motion to ask for a medical examination and is considering to withdraw that motion. The Chamber would prefer this to be done in writing; one or two lines could do. The next item is about the witness order. The Chamber received this morning a short list, called "Witness Order for the Period of 6 to 14 December, 2006." May I take it that this is the witness order the parties agree upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that -- and I'm just now using not their names. That means the first one, being VS-1133; second one, VS-1136; the third, VS-1134; the fourth, VS-1135; then one witness by videolink. I think at this moment it could only be VS-053, because no decisions have yet been taken in respect of VS-1141. Sixth on the list is VS-017, and seventh is the expert witness, Ewa Tabeau. Mr. Hooper, yesterday, the Prosecution filed additional information in respect of Witness 1141, but that was mainly focussing on a videolink. There is a motion which also asks for variance of protective measures. If you'd still like to respond to that, you will have an opportunity to do so, of course, if you'd like to respond now, because I don't think we received any early response. But I'm not quite sure that the motion was translated and brought to the attention of Mr. Seselj. I must even assume that it has not been done. Therefore, if you'd like to respond to that, if could be done, I take it, only in private session at least, if you would like to go to the content of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: We would still prefer that positive medical evidence be provided in respect of that witness, that he be seen -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry. Can you give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would prefer to do it in writing this afternoon, then, of course, we would --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Yes, in the circumstances, we will. There's a certain amount of confusion, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps even before official filing, a courtesy copy to the Prosecution and perhaps even a message to the legal officers of the Chamber might expedite decision-making on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We're talking about the same witness but a different measure. There's no objection to face and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's then clear. I have to look exactly whether that is what additionally had been asked. I think it was. Yes, I see nodding from the side of the Prosecution. There's one issue I'd like to briefly mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. While we're still on the topic of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to inform the Chamber, yesterday I raised the matter of the scope of the testimony of expert witness Dr. Ewa Tabeau, should we reach her in December, and yesterday, there was discussions amongst the parties, and after full and frank and earnest negotiations, it was decided that if Ms. Tabeau testifies in December, the evidence will only pertain to her expert report related to migrations from Vojvodina, in particular, the town of Hrtkovci. So she would testify at another time about her Bosnia report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you said that -- that it was decided that she would testify. I take it that you said so in anticipation that the Chamber would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Can I just indicate that it wasn't until yesterday that we had access to the exhibits of VS-054, all the exhibits, and it wasn't until last night that I was able to complete reading them. Our position on VS-054 is, therefore, open to discussion. The Prosecution had sought his attendance in the first session, and I don't burden the Chamber more with that, merely to indicate that by the time we leave here this morning, with your blessing, we will confirm one way or the other the full ordering of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. VS-054 is not at this moment on the list that was agreed upon, but I do understand that it would be a replacement, if there are any slots. Is that correct? But the parties still have to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If that became necessary, we would certainly do our best to bring VS-054 here, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but is not -- this witness is not on the list a this moment, so we do not at this moment expect anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Chamber will consider the present situation. We have now seven people on the list. I have not left yet the area of witnesses. The Chamber noticed that last week, at least it was told to us yesterday, there had been a communication between the Prosecution and Mr. Hooper/Mr. O'Shea relating to the order of witnesses. The Chamber noticed that that was at the time when Mr. Seselj was still self-represented. Therefore, the appropriate way of dealing and discussing the order of witnesses at that time would have been with Mr. Seselj, because I take it it was not during the Status Conference that such communication took place. Of course, meanwhile, the procedural situation has changed and therefore we'll proceed on the basis as -- meanwhile, after last week's communication, on the basis of the agreement reached between the parties which now has been approved by the Chamber. I just want to stress how important it is always to act exactly in the context of the then-existing procedural situation, as far as representation is concerned. Is there any other matter the parties want to raise at this moment? Because if we adjourn today, it will be until the 6th of December, when the Chamber expects that the first witnesses will be called. I see nodding "no." I take that as a negative answer from the Prosecution side. Mr. Hooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: Give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOOPER
utterances.text: There are no other matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until the 6th of December, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of December, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: [The accused is not present in the courtroom]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.33 a.m.,
